common_name: Blue Chiffon Rose of Sharon (Blue-Lavender Double Anemone-Form Shrub Althea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Chiffon is part of the Proven Winners ColorChoice Chiffon series bred for a frilly, anemone-form double bloom that sets little to no seed.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where this vigorous, upright rose of Sharon tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil once established. Blue Chiffon opens 4-5 inch single, soft blue-lavender flowers with a frilly tuft of smaller petals rising from the center of each bloom, giving the anemone-form look shared by its white, pink, and lavender Chiffon-series siblings, and covers the shrub with color from early summer well into fall. Because the Chiffon series was selected for reduced seed set compared to older rose of Sharon types, cleanup of volunteer seedlings is far lighter than with heirloom althea. Prune lightly in late winter to shape, since Blue Chiffon blooms on new wood and tolerates hard pruning if an older plant needs rejuvenation.

common_name: Blush Satin Rose of Sharon (Light Pink Red-Eyed Single-Flowered Shrub Althea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Blush Satin (patented as Hibiscus syriacus 'Mathilde', US PP12,660) is part of the Proven Winners ColorChoice Satin series of single-flowered rose of Sharon.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Blush Satin is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and shrugs off the heavy clay and poor soil common to Gulf Coast landscapes. Large single blooms open a soft, light pink with a prominent dark red central eye, held against glossy dark-green foliage, and the shrub buds heavily for a long late-summer display that begins later than many older rose of Sharon selections. It grows into a tall, vase-shaped specimen useful as an informal hedge, screen, or specimen shrub, and like other Satin-series selections it is noticeably less prone to self-sowing than seed-grown heirloom althea. Prune in late winter to control size, since flowers form on the current season's new growth.

common_name: Heartthrob Hardy Hibiscus (Dark Red-Black Giant-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown crowns in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Heartthrob (US Plant Patent PP24,760) is a Walters Gardens introduction prized for its unusually dark, near-black-red flower color.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, since hardy hibiscus is a wetland native that flowers best and grows most vigorously with steady moisture through the summer. Heartthrob produces enormous 8-9 inch flowers in a smoldering dark red that shades toward black at the base of each petal, giving the bloom unusual depth of color compared to the brighter clear reds of older moscheutos cultivars, and holds its well-branched clump upright without staking. Bloom runs from early summer through the end of the season on new growth, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies to the large, saucer-shaped flowers held above the foliage. Cut the dead canes to the ground after hard frost and mulch the crown for winter, and expect new growth to emerge later in spring than most perennial neighbors.

common_name: Double Confederate Rose (Flore Pleno Cotton Rose, Color-Changing Double-Flowered Shrub)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring after frost danger passes in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Flore Pleno' (also sold as 'Plena' or 'Plenus') is the classic fully double form of the heirloom Confederate rose long passed hand to hand through Deep South gardens.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring after frost danger passes, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, where it quickly grows into a large, multi-stemmed shrub-tree. 'Flore Pleno' bears fully double, peony-like 4-6 inch flowers that open white to pale pink in the morning, blush deeper pink by midday, and deepen to rose-red by evening, so a single autumn shrub can carry all three color stages of bloom at once. This double form is the classic heirloom sold and passed along across the Gulf South for generations, distinct from solid-colored selections like 'Rubrum' that forgo the single-day color shift for one steady hue. Like the species it dies back to the ground after hard freezes in zone 7-8 but resprouts vigorously from the root crown each spring and flowers heavily from late summer into fall; prune the prior year's growth back hard in late winter to keep the large shrub in scale.
